records.title: Caregiver rotation for exhaustion prevention
records.category: Anatomy · Biology · Medicine · Tools · Repair · Construction
records.summary: A rotation method for caring for children, elderly people, sick people, injured people, and anxious group members without burning out one person.
records.content: One reliable caregiver often becomes the entire system until they collapse. A rotation protects both the vulnerable person and the caregiver. Write the care tasks: water, food, medicine timing, hygiene, bathroom help, comfort, observation, sleep, and communication. Split tasks into short blocks. Keep a handover note so the next person knows what happened. The caregiver off duty should actually rest, eat, drink, and warm or cool down. Exhaustion causes mistakes with medicine, water, conflict, and safety.

Assign short shifts instead of open-ended duty.
Write handover notes after each shift.
Protect rest for the off-duty caregiver.
Escalate early if the caregiver becomes confused, angry, shaky, or unable to focus.
warnings: Do not let one exhausted person control medicine, heat, movement, and decisions alone.

records.title: Basic wound cleaning decision path
records.category: Anatomy · Biology · Medicine · Tools · Repair · Construction
records.summary: A cautious, non-surgical guide for protecting a minor wound from dirt, delayed cleaning, and unsafe improvised treatment.
records.content: A wound is not only a cut; it is an opening for dirt, bacteria, chemicals, and later infection. The safest first goal is simple: stop dangerous bleeding, keep the person calm, wash hands, remove loose surface dirt with clean water, cover with the cleanest available dressing, and watch for worsening signs. Deep wounds, bites, dirty punctures, crush injuries, heavy bleeding, loss of feeling, exposed structures, spreading redness, fever, bad smell, or severe pain need qualified medical care as soon as possible. Do not pour harsh chemicals into wounds. Do not close dirty deep wounds with glue, thread, or tape. Record time, cause, cleaning, dressing changes, pain, redness, swelling, and fever.
steps: Check for severe bleeding and seek emergency help if present.
Wash hands or use gloves before touching the wound.
Rinse loose dirt with clean water.
Cover with a clean dressing and keep it protected.
Change dressing when wet, dirty, or loose.
Record changes and watch for infection signs.
warnings: This is not a replacement for professional medical care.
Do not close deep dirty wounds yourself.
Do not use fuel, bleach, strong cleaners, soil, ash, or unknown powders in a wound.

Mark slippery areas.

warnings: Do not climb during active storm conditions.
Do not hide wet materials inside walls or under sealed plastic for long periods.
Water near electricity is a serious hazard.

records.title: Clay brick drying rack routine

records.content: Clay brick drying rack routine helps a group turn wet clay pieces into usable building units without rushing the process and cracking half the batch. Start by writing the soil source, added sand or fiber, molding date, and weather notes in a notebook. Set the fresh bricks on a flat raised rack, board, or woven platform so they do not wick extra ground moisture. Leave finger-width gaps between pieces so air moves around all sides. Shade them from hard midday sun at first, because fast surface drying can split the outside while the center stays weak. Turn each brick gently after the first firming stage and mark damaged bricks for repair, grinding, or noncritical use. Check one sample each day for edge strength, center moisture, and visible warping before moving the batch toward final drying or low-risk test use.

Test the final soap on tools, cloth, or dirty hands in a controlled way before relying on it for regular hygiene. Choose a site above obvious flood lines and watch how water behaves after rain before relying on the pit. Use raised supports, baskets, shelves, or divided sections so containers do not sit in standing dampness. Keep a written map or list of what is inside, because forgotten stores become rot, pests, or dangerous surprises. Inspect the pit regularly for smell changes, roof weakness, water seepage, insect pressure, and signs that humans are opening it too often during the hottest hours. Use the coolest storage for the items that truly need it and leave breathing space around containers.

records.title: Shared childcare quiet hour
records.summary: A supervised quiet period in a shared shelter or community space gives children and caregivers a predictable pause without isolating anyone. This card sets the room, supervision, check-in, accessibility, and handover rules needed to keep the period calm and safe.
records.content:
Core procedure:
1. Choose a clean, ventilated, low-traffic area that keeps exits open and preserves direct sightlines between supervisors and children. 2. Post the exact start and finish time, the responsible adults, the maximum group size, and the authorised pickup procedure before admitting children. 3. Confirm each child’s name, caregiver, communication or accessibility needs, known allergies, comfort item, and agreed location after the quiet period. 4. Offer low-noise choices such as drawing, reading, puzzles, headphones, or rest; do not require sleep or punish a child who cannot remain silent. 5. Maintain the agreed supervision ratio, complete head counts at entry, midpoint, and exit, and keep toilet trips or room changes recorded. 6. At closing, release each child only to the recorded caregiver, note any concern or missing item, clean shared surfaces, and brief the next team. Primary safety boundary: Never leave children unsupervised, lock them in, block an exit, use restraint as behaviour control, or release a child to an unverified person. Fallback: If a separate room is unavailable, mark a quiet corner within the main supervised area and use staggered small groups.
materials: drinking water and basic cleaning supplies
warnings: Never leave children unsupervised, lock them in, block an exit, use restraint as behaviour control, or release a child to an unverified person.
Protect privacy: display only the minimum operational information and keep medical, family, and contact details out of public view.
common_mistakes: Starting without a named supervisor and pickup list
Mixing very different age or sensory needs without enough staff
Treating quiet time as forced sleep or punishment
Ending without a head count and caregiver handover
alternatives: If a separate room is unavailable, mark a quiet corner within the main supervised area and use staggered small groups.
If staffing is insufficient, shorten the session and require each caregiver to remain with their own child.
failure_signs: A child cannot be accounted for or an unauthorised person attempts pickup
Supervision falls below the planned level or sightlines are lost
Distress, bullying, unsafe temperature, smoke, crowding, or an evacuation instruction develops
when_not_to_use: Do not run the session during an active evacuation, fire, security threat, missing-child search, or other event requiring everyone’s immediate attention.
This card does not replace qualified safeguarding, medical, disability-support, or mental-health care.
records.short_term: Run one short supervised session, verify every handover, and record what changed before the next session.
records.long_term: Create a rotating caregiver roster, age-appropriate activity boxes, accessibility notes, and a practised reunification procedure.
records.if_method_fails: Stop admission, keep the current children together under direct supervision, contact their recorded caregivers, and move the group to the main safe area.
records.environment_notes: Reduce noise and bright light where possible, keep mobility routes clear, and provide visual or simple-language instructions for children who need them.

records.title: Elderly neighbor welfare rotation
records.summary: A respectful check-in rotation for older neighbors during heat, cold, outage, smoke, water cut, or isolation without exposing private medical details.
records.content: Core sequence: 1) List only the address, preferred contact method, check time, and practical support agreed by the person. 2) Use two short check windows per day and mark no-answer separately from refused help. 3) Ask about water, temperature, phone charge, medicines available today, and whether a trusted contact should be called. 4) Escalate to family, building manager, local authority, or 112 when there is danger, repeated no-answer, confusion, or unsafe indoor heat or cold.

records.title: Family reunification plan with three meeting levels
records.summary: Use a nearby point, neighbourhood point, and out-of-area destination so the family has options when one zone is inaccessible.
records.content: Action sequence: Choose one safe point immediately outside the home, one outside the neighbourhood, and one outside the affected area. For each point write the trigger, route, transport, accessibility, animal policy, contact person, and waiting time. Agree that everyone sends status to one outside contact rather than repeatedly calling each other. Practise a weekday, night, school, and no-phone version of the plan. Safety boundary: Do not select a meeting point in a flood channel, dense vegetation, fuel area, unstable building, or traffic hazard. Do not keep changing the plan through separate messages; one person must own the current version.

Safety boundary: Do not forward urgent-looking content merely because many people sent it. Do not reveal private identities or locations while correcting a rumour.

records.summary: Prepare a factual packet for police, 112, responders, and trusted search coordinators without launching an unsafe informal search.
records.content: Action sequence: Record full name, age, appearance, clothing, phone, vehicle, mobility, communication, medical urgency, and any immediate hazard. Safety boundary: Do not enter floodwater, fire zones, unstable structures, cliffs, caves, or restricted terrain to search without trained coordination. Do not publish sensitive medical, identity, or location details more widely than necessary.

records.title: Neighbour check-in without creating dependency or confusion
records.summary: Coordinate brief consent-based checks for isolated or vulnerable neighbours while keeping clear limits and emergency escalation.
records.content: Action sequence: Ask in advance who wants a check, preferred method, emergency contact, access need, animal, medicine, or device concern. Use a fixed check window and a simple status: okay, needs practical help, needs qualified help, or no response. For no response, follow the agreed sequence of call, trusted contact, building manager or neighbour, and emergency service when risk justifies it. Record only necessary facts and close each request with a named next action. Safety boundary: Do not enter a home, handle medicine, move a person, or operate utilities beyond consent and training. Do not promise continuous monitoring that the group cannot reliably provide.

warnings: Do not enter a home, handle medicine, move a person, or operate utilities beyond consent and training.

records.title: Bilingual emergency notice for a shared building
records.summary: Post a short Greek-English notice with source, time, affected area, required action, assistance point, and next update.
records.content: Action sequence: Use a clear title such as EVACUATE, SHELTER INSIDE, WATER NOT SAFE, POWER HAZARD, or NEXT UPDATE. Write source, publication time, exact floors or areas, action, route, meeting point, accessibility help, contact, and next review time. Use large lettering, simple symbols, high contrast, and both Greek and English. Remove or cross out the notice visibly when it expires and replace it with a dated correction. Safety boundary: Do not invent an authority, instruction, shelter, or route. Do not leave an outdated notice in place after conditions change.

Keep the bitten limb still and below heart level if comfortable.
Remove rings or tight items before swelling.
Do not cut, suck, burn, ice, or apply chemicals.
Call poison/emergency services and transport calmly.

records.title: Large burn area evacuation priority
records.content: Large, deep, face, hand, foot, genital, inhalation, chemical, or electrical burns need urgent professional care.
steps: Stop the burning source safely.
Cool minor thermal burns with clean cool running water if available, but do not cause hypothermia.
Remove tight items before swelling if they are not stuck.
Cover with clean non-fluffy material.
Do not apply butter, oils, powders, toothpaste, or dirty creams.

records.title: Chest pain and stroke no-delay board
records.content: Heart attack and stroke signs need immediate transport decisions; waiting for certainty can cost the treatment window.
steps: Treat chest pressure, severe shortness of breath, sweating, faintness, one-sided weakness, face droop, speech trouble, sudden severe headache, or new confusion as urgent.
Record exact last-known-well time.
Do not let the person drive themselves.
Keep them calm, seated or positioned comfortably.
Send medicine list and allergies with them.

records.title: Seizure cluster escalation card
records.content: Most seizure support is about safety, timing, recovery position, and escalation when seizures repeat or do not stop.
steps: Protect from nearby hazards without holding the person down.
Time the seizure.
Do not put anything in the mouth.
After movement stops, keep airway clear and monitor breathing.
Escalate for first seizure, injury, pregnancy, water exposure, repeated seizures, long duration, breathing trouble, or not waking normally.

records.title: Radiological contamination medical check-in
records.content: Radiological events require sheltering, removing outer contamination, gentle washing, instructions, and symptom records; panic evacuation can increase exposure.
steps: Get inside, stay inside, and tune to official instructions if possible.
Remove outer clothing carefully if contamination is suspected and bag it away from people.
Wash exposed skin gently with soap and water if available; do not scrub harshly.
Keep dust out of mouth, nose, wounds, and food.
Record location, time outside, wounds, vomiting, burns, and official instructions received.

records.title: Chemical plume symptom and exposure log
records.content: After a chemical release, symptoms and exposure details help poison centers and doctors; guessing the chemical can waste time.
steps: Shelter-in-place or evacuate according to official instruction and wind direction if known.
Record odor, visible cloud, location, wind, time, symptoms, and contaminated clothing.
Separate exposed people from clean zones when safe.
Do not induce vomiting or give random antidotes.
Call poison/emergency services with the log.

records.title: Chemical splash skin and eye emergency
records.content: Chemical exposure needs fast decontamination, protection of helpers, and poison/emergency instructions.
steps: Protect helpers from the chemical first.
Remove contaminated clothing if safe and avoid spreading chemical.
Rinse affected skin or eyes with clean running water when official guidance supports flushing.
Do not neutralize chemicals with other chemicals.
Keep container labels or photos for professionals.

records.title: Diabetes collapse medicine-and-food log
records.content: Diabetes emergencies are worsened by missed meals, stress, infection, heat, medicine loss, and no refrigeration. Records prevent dangerous guessing.
steps: Keep the person’s own plan, medicines, meter, strips, snacks, and emergency contacts together.
Record meals, vomiting, illness, activity, symptoms, and medicine timing.
Do not change insulin or prescription doses without professional guidance.
Escalate for unconsciousness, confusion, repeated vomiting, breathing changes, severe weakness, or very abnormal readings if known.
Protect insulin and supplies from heat, freezing, and theft.

records.title: Dialysis missed-treatment emergency route
records.content: People depending on dialysis need an early route plan before roads, phones, or clinics fail completely.
steps: Keep dialysis schedule, clinic contacts, diagnosis, access type, medicines, diet limits, and transport options in a waterproof folder.
Contact clinic or emergency services early after a missed session.
Do not improvise dialysis or catheter care.
Escalate for breathing trouble, chest pain, confusion, severe weakness, swelling, or no urine changes.
Plan backup transport and nearest open facility.

records.title: Palliative comfort when evacuation is impossible
records.content: When rescue is delayed and cure is impossible, comfort, dignity, family contact, hygiene, and truthful records still matter.
steps: Do not abandon the person.
Keep them clean, warm/cool, positioned comfortably, and protected from crowds.
Offer sips only if safe to swallow.
Support spiritual, family, or cultural wishes when safe.
Do not give medicines outside prescription or professional advice.
Record changes and attempts to reach help.

records.title: Remote doctor radio handover packet
records.content: When only a radio or weak phone works, a structured handover saves time and reduces dangerous missing details.
steps: Prepare identity, age, sex if relevant, location, main problem, start time, red flags, vital observations if known, medicines, allergies, conditions, and actions taken.
Speak slowly and repeat critical numbers.
Ask the professional to repeat key instructions.
Write the advice with time and name/call sign if available.
Do not invent measurements.

records.title: Crowd crush medical prevention and response
records.content: Crowd crush is a medical emergency caused by pressure, not panic. Prevention is spacing, exits, and early movement away from pressure.
steps: Avoid dense chokepoints, fences, narrow stairs, and blocked exits.
If pressure builds, keep arms in front of chest and move diagonally with the flow when possible.
After escape, check breathing, chest pain, crush injury, fainting, and trauma.
Do not send crowds toward casualty areas.
Mark exits and one-way lanes in shelters.

records.title: Respectful deceased-person medical boundary
records.content: Death management in collapse must protect dignity, identification, infection control, and family information without unsafe handling.
steps: Confirm there is no immediate rescue or resuscitation role for lay helpers before shifting to deceased care.
Do not move the body unless safety, dignity, or official instruction requires it.
Record location, time found, identifying items, and who witnessed.
Use gloves/barriers and hand hygiene.
Protect from animals, weather, and public viewing while awaiting authorities or community process.

records.title: Infant and elder dehydration red flags
records.content: Infants and elders can deteriorate quickly from vomiting, diarrhea, heat, fever, or poor intake.
steps: Track drinking, wet diapers or urine, tears, mouth dryness, alertness, fever, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Prioritize safe fluids and professional advice early.
Keep them cool in heat and warm in cold.
Escalate urgently for no urine, lethargy, sunken eyes, repeated vomiting, blood, severe fever, or confusion.
Do not force large amounts if choking or vomiting risk is high.

records.title: Field dental emergency red flags
records.content: Dental problems can become face, airway, or bloodstream emergencies. This entry flags what needs urgent help.
steps: Escalate for facial swelling, fever, trouble swallowing, trouble breathing, spreading redness, eye swelling, trauma, uncontrolled bleeding, or immune weakness.
Keep mouth clean with safe water when possible.
Do not lance abscesses or pull teeth without qualified care.
Avoid placing aspirin or chemicals on gums.
Record pain start, swelling, fever, trauma, and medicines.

records.title: Knocked-out tooth transport rule
records.content: A knocked-out permanent tooth may be time-sensitive. The goal is clean handling and urgent dental care, not home dentistry.
steps: Confirm it is not a baby tooth before any reimplantation decision; when unsure, seek dental help.
Handle by the crown, not the root.
Keep it moist using dentist-recommended method or milk/saliva container if professional guidance is unavailable.
Do not scrub the root.
Get urgent dental care and record time out.

records.title: Disaster clinic infection control station
records.content: Even a basic care point needs clean/dirty zones, hand hygiene, sharps control, waste flow, and sick-person separation.
steps: Place hand hygiene at entrance and exit.
Separate wound care, respiratory symptoms, stomach illness, and medicine records if space allows.
Keep clean supplies off the floor and away from waste.
Use a sharps container or rigid labeled container for needles and blades.
Assign one person to watch cleaning schedule.

records.title: Referral queue red-flag sorting
records.content: When many people wait for care, a visible red-flag queue prevents quiet high-risk cases from being ignored.
steps: Create categories: immediate danger, urgent today, can wait with recheck, information only.
Use observations, not diagnoses.
Recheck waiting people regularly.
Move vulnerable people out of heat/cold/crowds.
Document who was referred, when, where, and by whom.

records.title: Long-term collapse clinic registry
records.content: A community without normal clinics needs a registry for chronic illness, pregnancy, infants, disabilities, medicines, allergies, and follow-up dates.
steps: Create opt-in confidential records with minimal necessary details.
List high-risk people and what support keeps them stable.
Track medicine supply, device power needs, mobility needs, and referral routes.
Review weekly or after any disaster event.
Keep backup paper copies protected from theft and weather.

records.title: Medical volunteer role verification board
records.content: In collapse, false confidence is dangerous. Roles should match verified training and tasks should have boundaries.
steps: Ask volunteers what training they have and what they are not trained to do.
Assign non-clinical helpers to records, cleaning, transport, supplies, translation, and crowd control.
Do not let unverified people perform invasive tasks.
Pair new helpers with experienced people.
Remove any helper who ignores consent, hygiene, or safety boundaries.

records.title: Elderly delirium disaster trigger list
records.content: New confusion in elders can come from infection, dehydration, heat, cold, medicine problems, pain, or low oxygen.
steps: Treat sudden confusion as a danger sign, not stubbornness.
Check recent fluids, urine, fever, pain, falls, medicines, sleep, heat, and cold exposure.
Move to quiet lighted space with a familiar person.
Avoid restraints unless immediate life safety requires it.
Escalate for rapid change, weakness, breathing trouble, fever, fall, or inability to drink.

records.title: Heat stroke emergency cooling priority
records.content: In Greek summer, heat stroke is a true emergency: confusion, collapse, hot body, seizures, or inability to drink needs rapid cooling and emergency help.
steps: Move to shade or a cool room immediately.
Call emergency help
Cool with water on skin, fans, wet cloths, and removing excess clothing when safe.
Do not give drink to someone confused, unconscious, or vomiting.
Track time and response to cooling.

records.title: Severe hypothermia gentle handling
records.content: Severely cold people can be fragile; rough movement, alcohol, and fast unsafe heating can worsen danger.
steps: Move out of wind and wet conditions.
Handle gently and keep horizontal if possible.
Remove wet clothing only if it can be done without rough movement.
Warm the body core with dry layers, blankets, and shared warm space.
Seek urgent professional help for confusion, shivering stops, weak pulse, unconsciousness, or very cold body.

records.title: Life threat priority scan in extreme isolation
records.content: Focus first on dangers that can kill before help arrives: unsafe scene, airway/breathing trouble, major bleeding, unconsciousness, shock signs, severe heat/cold exposure, poisoning, or rapid worsening. This is not medical advice; it is a safety and organization checklist until qualified help is available.
steps: Stop and look for hazards before touching anyone.
Call or send for help while basic support starts.
Handle heavy bleeding, breathing trouble, and unconsciousness as top priority.
Keep notes short and factual.
Recheck because quiet can mean worse, not better.

records.title: Newborn danger signs in disaster shelter
records.content: Newborns become cold, dehydrated, or infected quickly in shelters. Early escalation is the useful action.
steps: Keep newborn warm, dry, and close to caregiver.
Prioritize clean hands before touching baby or feeding items.
Escalate for poor feeding, fever or very cold body, fast or difficult breathing, blue/gray color, limpness, repeated vomiting, no wet diapers, or unusual sleepiness.
Avoid crowded sick zones.
Record feeding and diaper times.

records.title: Body fluid cleanup after mass injury
records.content: Blood, vomit, feces, and other fluids can spread infection and panic. Cleanup needs barriers, zoning, and disposal before normal activity returns.
steps: Block the area from children, animals, food, and foot traffic.
Wear gloves or the best available barrier.
Use absorbent material and dispose in labeled waste.
Clean hands and contaminated tools afterward.
Ventilate and record if exposure occurred.

records.title: Blood exposure log for helpers
records.content: Helpers who contact blood or body fluids need a record and professional advice, especially with cuts, eyes, mouth, or needle injury.
steps: Wash skin exposures with soap and clean water.
Flush eye or mouth exposure with clean water if available and safe.
Record time, fluid type, route, wound, and source if known.
Seek professional advice for bloodborne infection risk.
Do not shame the helper; exposure reporting protects everyone.

records.title: Sterile versus clean limits in collapse
records.content: Clean is not the same as sterile. This entry prevents false confidence and avoids unsafe invasive care.
steps: Use clean hands, clean water, clean cloth, and clean surfaces for basic care.
Do not call something sterile unless it was properly sterilized and stored.
Do not perform invasive procedures because supplies look clean.
Keep wound care separate from toilets, trash, animals, and cooking.
Refer deep wounds, foreign bodies, severe infection, and surgical needs.

records.title: Floodwater wound infection watch
records.content: Floodwater can carry sewage, chemicals, sharp debris, and bacteria. Open wounds need cleaning, covering, and early escalation for infection signs.
steps: Avoid floodwater contact with open wounds.
Wash with soap and clean water when available.
Cover clean open wounds with waterproof clean covering if available.
Watch redness, swelling, warmth, pus, bad smell, fever, increasing pain, or red streaks.
Record tetanus vaccine status if known.

records.title: Dirty puncture wound tetanus risk record
records.content: Dirty puncture, crush, burn, bite, soil, feces, saliva, and flood wounds need careful cleaning records and professional vaccine review.
steps: Write wound cause, time, contamination, and cleaning done.
Clean visible dirt with clean water when available.
Do not rely on antibiotics to prevent tetanus without medical guidance.
Seek professional review for tetanus vaccination and wound care.
Recheck for infection signs daily.

records.title: Human and animal bite escalation card
records.content: Bites can hide deep infection, tendon injury, rabies risk, tetanus risk, and legal reporting issues.
steps: Get away from the animal or attacker safely.
Wash the bite with soap and clean water if available.
Control bleeding with clean pressure.
Seek urgent professional advice for bites to hand, face, genitals, deep punctures, immune weakness, unknown animal, or worsening symptoms.
Record animal description and owner if safe.

records.title: Sepsis suspicion escalation checklist
records.content: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection. This guide helps spot deterioration and move fast without pretending to diagnose.
steps: Watch for infection plus confusion, extreme weakness, fast breathing, pale/mottled skin, very hot or cold body, severe pain, low urine, or rapid decline.
Treat as urgent transport priority.
Record source of infection, fever pattern, urine, alertness, and medicines.
Keep warm, safe, and monitored.
Do not wait for all signs to appear.

records.title: Mass casualty first thirty minutes board
records.summary: Organizes the first half hour after an event with many injured people when professional help is delayed.
records.content: In a mass casualty event, chaos kills through duplicated effort, blocked exits, missed breathing problems, and missing information. Create one visible board with scene dangers, helper roles, casualty count, urgent transport names, supply needs, and time of last check. The board does not diagnose; it keeps people from disappearing into the crowd.
steps: Choose one calm coordinator and one recorder.
Mark unsafe zones, exits, and a quiet casualty collection point.
Count people without crowding them.
Record red flags first: breathing trouble, heavy bleeding, unconsciousness, severe burns, crush injury, pregnancy danger, infant distress.
Send runners for help, water, lights, blankets, and transport.
Recheck every listed person on a fixed schedule.

records.title: Extreme medical disclaimer and red-line rules
records.summary: A clear safety boundary for using the medical section during collapse, isolation, or no-ambulance conditions.
records.content: Place this warning before any extreme medical entry. The database can help organize first response, records, hygiene, transport, and escalation, but it cannot examine a person, diagnose illness, prescribe medicine, or replace a clinician. In worst-case conditions, the safest goal is to reduce immediate harm, avoid contamination, record changes, preserve dignity, and reach trained help as early as possible.
steps: Read this before acting on any medical entry.
Use the guide to organize safety, hygiene, records, comfort, and transport.
Treat breathing trouble, heavy bleeding, unconsciousness, poisoning, severe burns, pregnancy danger signs, infants in distress, or fast worsening as urgent.
Do not improvise surgery, diagnosis, prescription changes, or invasive procedures.
Write who did what, when, and why so a professional can review later.

records.title: Medicine rationing ethics ledger
records.content: When medicines are scarce, secret decisions cause conflict and harm. A ledger creates transparency without giving untrained dosing advice.
steps: Inventory medicines by name, strength, owner, expiry, storage need, and prescription status.
Do not share prescription medicines without professional guidance.
Prioritize the medicine owner and life-sustaining continuity plans.
Use a small review group for scarce common supplies.
Record every decision and reason.

records.title: Antibiotics no-sharing collapse rule
records.content: Antibiotics can fail or harm when used for the wrong illness, dose, person, allergy, or duration.
steps: Do not share leftover antibiotics.
Do not use antibiotics for every fever, cough, or wound without medical guidance.
Record allergies and previous severe reactions.
Seek professional advice for infected wounds, severe illness, pregnancy, infants, immune weakness, and worsening symptoms.
Protect stored medicines from heat, moisture, and children.

records.title: Pain medicine safety under stress
records.content: Pain, fear, and fatigue make overdose and dangerous mixing more likely. This entry keeps decisions tied to labels and professionals.
steps: Use only medicines the person can safely take and only according to label or clinician instructions.
Do not mix with alcohol or unknown sedatives.
Check duplicate ingredients in cold/flu products.
Record time and amount from the label without guessing.
Escalate if pain is severe, new, worsening, after trauma, chest/abdominal, or with confusion.

records.title: Self-harm immediate safety circle
records.content: When someone may harm themselves, the first task is not debate; it is reducing immediate danger and connecting them to live help.
steps: Stay with the person or assign a calm trusted adult if safe.
Move weapons, poisons, ropes, medicines, and other immediate means away without confrontation.
Call emergency services or crisis support.
Use simple statements: you are not alone, help is coming, stay with me.
Do not shame, challenge, or leave them isolated.

records.title: Panic and dissociation grounding in shelter
records.content: Crowds, explosions, grief, and sleep loss can trigger panic or dissociation. Practical grounding helps until professional support is available.
steps: Move to a quieter safer edge of the shelter.
Speak slowly and use the person’s name if known.
Ask them to notice feet on floor, one object they see, one sound, and one slow breath.
Offer water only if fully alert and safe to swallow.
Escalate if chest pain, fainting, self-harm risk, psychosis, or medical symptoms appear.

records.title: Mass diarrhea dehydration station
records.content: When many people have diarrhea or vomiting, the survival task is clean water, separate toilets, hand hygiene, fluid access, and red-flag referral.
steps: Separate sick toilet area from kitchen and water storage.
Use safe water and official oral rehydration packets/instructions when available.
Track urine, drinking ability, vomiting, blood in stool, fever, and alertness.
Prioritize infants, elders, pregnancy, and chronic illness.
Clean hands and surfaces after every toilet or cleanup task.

records.title: Shelter outbreak isolation lanes
records.content: A crowded shelter needs clean lanes for healthy, exposed, sick, and recovering people to slow spread without abandoning care.
steps: Create separate sleeping and toilet zones if space allows.
Assign dedicated helpers for sick zones when possible.
Keep masks, ventilation, hand hygiene, and waste control visible.
Do not mix food service with sick care.
Post clear rules in both languages.

records.title: Fever with rash danger watch
records.content: Fever with rash can be harmless or dangerous; in collapse, isolate gently and escalate red flags instead of guessing.
steps: Keep the person away from crowded sleeping and food zones.
Record fever start, rash appearance, travel, contacts, medicines, and vaccination history if known.
Escalate urgently for stiff neck, confusion, purple rash, breathing trouble, severe headache, pregnancy, infant, immune weakness, or rapid worsening.
Use hygiene barriers and ventilation.
Do not scrape or apply random chemicals.

records.title: Quarantine ethics and care minimums
records.content: Isolation without care becomes punishment. Even in outbreak collapse, people need water, food, sanitation, communication, and dignity.
steps: Explain the reason and expected review time.
Provide safe water, food, toilet access, medicine support, and a way to ask for help.
Keep families informed without exposing private details.
Review isolation daily and end it when official/local health guidance allows.
Do not use quarantine to punish enemies or unwanted people.

records.title: Oxygen concentrator and powered medical device outage
records.content: Powered medical devices need a written outage plan: battery time, backup power, evacuation trigger, and contacts.
steps: List every powered medical device and battery runtime.
Keep charging schedule and backup power rules visible.
Tell utility, neighbors, and helpers before disasters when possible.
Move early before batteries are low if evacuation is needed.
Do not run generators indoors or near windows.

records.title: Pregnancy bleeding and preeclampsia warning card
steps: Escalate immediately for vaginal bleeding, severe belly pain, severe headache, vision changes, swelling with illness, seizures, fever, fainting, trouble breathing, or reduced fetal movement if known.
Keep pregnancy records, blood type if known, medicines, allergies, due date, and clinic contacts together.
Do not give random herbs or medicines.
Prepare transport early.
Protect privacy and a trusted support person.

records.title: No-ambulance childbirth clean boundary
records.content: If birth happens before help arrives, the safest layperson role is cleanliness, warmth, privacy, timing, and urgent help, not pulling or cutting.
steps: Call for help as early as possible.
Create a clean, warm, private area with clean towels or cloths.
Let the body progress naturally; do not pull the baby or cord.
Keep baby warm and skin-to-skin if safe.
Escalate immediately for heavy bleeding, seizures, severe pain, fever, baby not breathing, or placenta not delivered within local professional guidance time.

records.title: Postpartum hemorrhage danger response
records.content: Heavy bleeding after birth is an emergency. This entry focuses on calling help, tracking blood loss, warmth, and rapid transfer.
steps: Call emergency help immediately for heavy or continuous bleeding, faintness, pale skin, confusion, or weakness.
Track time and soaked cloths/pads without obsessing over exact volume.
Keep the person warm and lying safely.
Do not insert anything or give random medicines/herbs.
Send pregnancy and birth notes with the patient.

records.title: Casualty tag without medical diagnosis
records.summary: A simple tag that travels with a casualty when clinics, ambulances, or relatives are separated.
records.content: A casualty tag is not a diagnosis. It is a memory tool: name or description, age estimate, contact, allergies, medicines, known conditions, event time, red flags, actions taken, and last check. In collapse, a tag can prevent repeated mistakes and help the next helper understand what changed.
steps: Use pencil or waterproof marker if possible.
Attach the tag to clothing or a bag, not directly to skin.
Write observations, not guesses.
Update time whenever the person is rechecked or moved.
Keep private details covered from the public.

records.title: Dust asbestos and silica collapse breathing plan
records.content: Collapsed buildings can create hazardous dust. The safest medical action is avoidance, wet dust control, respiratory protection if available, and symptom tracking.
steps: Keep children, elders, pregnant people, and lung disease away from dusty debris.
Do not dry sweep suspected hazardous dust.
Use appropriate mask/respirator if available and fitted; cloth is not equal protection.
Ventilate away from clean sleeping/food areas.
Escalate for breathing trouble, chest pain, persistent cough, wheeze, or eye injury.

records.title: Sexual assault privacy and medical route
records.content: In extreme situations, survivors need safety, consent, privacy, evidence-aware choices, and urgent medical/psychological support without pressure.
steps: Move the survivor to safety if they want and it is safe.
Do not force them to talk, wash, report, or be examined.
Offer trusted support person, privacy, clean clothing, water, and transport options.
Seek professional care for injuries, pregnancy/STI concerns, forensic options, and mental support.
Record only what the survivor consents to record.

records.title: Medical supply cache under siege or isolation
records.content: Extreme isolation needs organized supplies: not secret hoarding, but protected stock with expiry checks, access rules, and transparent use.
steps: Separate wound care, hygiene, chronic medicine, respiratory, infant, and documentation supplies.
Store away from heat, damp, pests, and children.
Use first-expiring items first.
Keep a checkout ledger for scarce supplies.
Do not hide life-saving supplies from legitimate community emergency use.

records.title: Improvised stretcher transport safety
records.content: Bad transport can worsen injuries. The entry focuses on route safety, enough carriers, spine caution, and stopping if deterioration occurs.
steps: Do not move unless staying is more dangerous or transport is needed for care.
Choose the smoothest route before lifting.
Use enough carriers and one caller for commands.
Keep head, neck, and torso aligned when trauma is possible.
Stop if pain, breathing, bleeding, alertness, or limb feeling worsens.

records.title: Heavy bleeding pressure-and-handover routine
records.content: Extreme bleeding needs immediate pressure, calm role assignment, and fast professional escalation. The guide records times and actions without turning untrained people into surgeons.
steps: Use direct pressure with the cleanest available cloth or dressing.
Keep pressure steady and send someone for emergency help.
Do not repeatedly lift the dressing to look.
If trained and locally allowed, use bleeding-control equipment according to training only.
Record start time, visible blood loss, and changes.

records.title: Severed body part preservation boundary
records.content: For amputation-type injuries, the priority is the living person: bleeding control, shock prevention, urgent transport, and clean handling of the separated part without unsafe experiments.
steps: Care for the person first, especially bleeding and warmth.
Place the separated part in the cleanest available bag or wrapping.
Keep it cool if safe, but avoid direct contact with ice or dirty water.
Label time and identity.
Send it with the person to professional care.

records.title: Crush injury release warning card
records.content: After long entrapment under rubble, sudden release can be medically dangerous. The entry focuses on urgent rescue coordination, time records, warmth, and rapid professional care.
steps: Record how long the person may have been trapped.
Do not pull or lift debris unsafely; protect rescuers too.
Call professional rescue and medical help as early as possible.
Keep the person warm, calm, and still if safe.
Report crushed limb, dark urine, severe pain, weakness, or confusion urgently.

records.title: Impaled object do-not-pull rule
records.content: An object stuck in the body can be blocking bleeding. This entry prevents the common deadly mistake of pulling it out without trained care.
steps: Do not remove the object unless it blocks breathing and trained help says so.
Stabilize around it with bulky clean material.
Control bleeding around the injury without pressing the object deeper.
Keep the person still and warm.
Arrange urgent transport and write the time.

records.title: Open chest injury emergency escalation
records.content: Chest trauma with breathing trouble is a high-risk emergency. The goal is calm positioning, minimal handling, urgent care, and clear handover.
steps: Call emergency help immediately.
Let the person find the easiest breathing position unless spinal injury is suspected.
Cover obvious open wounds with the cleanest available material without pushing inside.
Watch breathing, skin color, consciousness, and worsening pain.
Prepare rapid handover.

records.title: Abdominal injury protection and no-food rule
records.content: Severe abdominal trauma can worsen with movement, food, drink, or pressure. This entry keeps the person still, protected, and ready for urgent care.
steps: Call emergency help
Do not give food, alcohol, or unnecessary medicine.
Cover exposed tissue with the cleanest moist clean barrier if trained supplies are available; do not push anything back inside.
Keep knees slightly supported if comfortable and trauma allows.
Watch for shock, worsening pain, pale skin, or confusion.

records.title: Open fracture contamination control
records.content: An open fracture is a major infection and bleeding risk. The entry focuses on covering, immobilizing without force, and urgent evacuation.
steps: Call for urgent care.
Do not push bone or tissue back in.
Cover with the cleanest available dressing.
Immobilize the limb in the position found if possible.
Check color, warmth, feeling, and movement beyond the injury without forcing.

records.title: Pelvic injury minimal movement rule
records.content: Falls, crushes, and vehicle impacts can hide pelvic bleeding. This entry prevents unnecessary movement and flags rapid evacuation.
steps: Suspect pelvic injury after major force, fall, crush, or severe hip/groin pain.
Do not repeatedly roll, sit, or walk the person.
Keep them still and warm.
Track pulse, alertness, skin color, and pain changes.
Get professional help for transport.

records.title: Blast injury hidden damage watch
records.content: Blast survivors may look okay while hearing, lungs, abdomen, or brain injury worsens later. The entry creates a delayed-symptom watch list.
steps: Move away from secondary hazards first.
Record distance from blast, time, and protection used.
Watch for breathing trouble, chest pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, hearing loss, severe headache, or bleeding.
Keep the person under observation even if they can walk.
Send urgent cases to professional care first.

records.title: Small cash envelope rotation
records.summary: A simple method for keeping emergency cash usable during card outages, bank closures, ferry disruption, fuel queues, or phone loss without advertising where money is kept.
records.content: Core sequence: 1) Split cash into daily-use and reserve envelopes so one mistake does not expose all money. 2) Use small notes for water, food, transport, phone charging, medicines, or official fees. 3) Record every use immediately because memory fails during queues and stress. 4) Check the envelope monthly and replace damaged notes or coins that are not accepted locally.
materials: small notes divided into two envelopes
expense log with date and reason
steps: Split cash into daily-use and reserve envelopes so one mistake does not expose all money.
Use small notes for water, food, transport, phone charging, medicines, or official fees.
Record every use immediately because memory fails during queues and stress.
Check the envelope monthly and replace damaged notes or coins that are not accepted locally.
related_topics: First five minutes household command reset

records.title: Household ransomware isolation and trusted recovery
records.summary: A non-technical containment sequence to disconnect affected devices, preserve information, use a clean device for account protection, and obtain trusted help without spreading the infection.
steps: Disconnect the suspected device from wired and wireless networks and external drives without exploring files or attaching new storage.
Photograph or write the message, time, device, recent actions, affected accounts, and any unusual alerts; preserve the device state for qualified help.

From a known-clean device, contact official organizational support, bank, email provider, or competent cyber authority and protect critical accounts with new unique credentials and multi-factor security.
Check offline backups before restoration, follow trusted recovery guidance, and monitor financial and identity accounts for secondary abuse.
warnings: Do not pay, negotiate, run random cleanup tools, or follow contact details supplied by the attacker without qualified advice.
Do not reconnect a restored device until containment and update steps are complete.

records.title: Disaster evidence photo and inventory log
records.summary: A safe documentation sequence for wide views, item details, serial information, dates, temporary repairs, expenses, and secure backup before cleanup changes the scene.
records.content: Use the materials as a compact field kit.
steps: Enter only after authorities and utility checks allow it; photograph the exterior and each room from safe positions before moving items.
Capture wide context, closer damage, model or serial information when reachable, water or soot lines, and a date-and-location note.
Number items in a written inventory and link each number to photographs, ownership evidence, estimated age, and immediate safety action.

records.title: First five minutes household command reset
records.summary: A short reset for the first five minutes after a shock, alarm, crash, smoke smell, violent weather, or unclear warning. It turns panic into a named caller, a safe meeting point, a head count, and one next action.
records.content: Use it when the situation is real but still manageable. Work slowly, keep one written decision log, and prefer the safest reversible action over a dramatic improvisation. Core sequence: 1) Say out loud what happened in one sentence and appoint one person to call or listen for official instructions. 2) Move everyone away from the immediate hazard before collecting bags, keys, shoes, or documents. 3) Count people, pets, mobility aids, essential medicines, and phones; write only missing items. 4) Choose one next action: shelter, leave, call 112, shut a safe utility, or wait for official instructions. Stop point: Do not use this reset to override an evacuation order, official shelter instruction, or immediate order from emergency responders. Main warnings: Do not send several people to investigate the same hazard while others are uncounted. Do not delay a 112 call for perfect details when life, fire, collapse, water, or violence is involved.

records.title: Food safety after refrigerator failure
records.category: Food · Agriculture · Psychology · Planning · Daily operations
records.summary: A cautious method for deciding what to eat first, what to cook, what to separate, and what to discard after power loss.
records.content: Food poisoning during a crisis can be worse than losing food. Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed, write the outage time, and decide in batches. High-risk foods include meat, seafood, dairy, soft cheeses, cooked rice, cooked pasta, leftovers, and opened prepared foods. Smell and appearance are not reliable safety tests. Cooking may kill many microbes but cannot reliably remove toxins already produced by some bacteria. Vulnerable people should receive the safest food, not questionable food. Separate doubtful items so they do not contaminate hands, utensils, shelves, or safe food.
steps: Write outage time and keep doors closed.
Group foods as shelf-stable, low-risk fresh, high-risk refrigerated, frozen, and leftovers.

Cook perishables only if they can be eaten soon without creating warm leftovers.
Discard food contaminated by floodwater, sewage, chemicals, leaks, swelling, or obvious spoilage.
Clean hands and surfaces after handling suspect food.
warnings: Do not trust smell alone for meat, dairy, rice, pasta, or leftovers.
Do not feed questionable food to children, elderly people, pregnant people, sick people, or pets.
Do not refreeze fully thawed high-risk food unless safe conditions are known.
common_mistakes: Opening the freezer repeatedly.
Cooking all thawing food at once and leaving it warm.
Letting leaking packages contaminate safe food.

records.title: Calm leadership during group stress
records.category: Food · Agriculture · Psychology · Planning · Daily operations
records.summary: How to keep a household or small group functional with short meetings, clear roles, and conflict reduction.
records.content: Stress makes groups freeze, argue, or rush. Calm leadership is not loud authority; it is structure. Use short meetings at fixed times. Start with facts, then needs, then tasks, then next review. Give people jobs they can finish. Avoid public humiliation. Keep children, elderly people, and anxious people informed with simple truth, not terrifying detail. Separate anger from decision making. Rotate unpleasant jobs. Praise completed tasks. A group that feels heard and organized wastes less food, water, battery, and energy.
steps: Hold short meetings at predictable times.
List confirmed facts before opinions.
Assign clear tasks with names and review times.
Rotate hard or unpleasant jobs.
Stop rumor chains by asking for source and confirmation.
End meetings with the next check-in time.
warnings: Do not use fear as the main motivator; it burns people out.
Do not let one person control all information.
Do not ignore quiet people; they may notice risks.
common_mistakes: Long meetings during exhaustion.
Giving vague tasks like help more.
Treating anxiety as disobedience.

Record burn location, approximate size, cause, time, pain, and any smoke inhalation risk. Get urgent help for burns on face, hands, feet, genitals, large areas, deep burns, chemical/electrical burns, breathing problems, or babies/elderly people. Do not break blisters or apply butter, oils, toothpaste, powders, or dirty creams.

records.title: Red-flag medical triage notebook
records.summary: A simple record system for deciding who needs urgent outside medical help first without pretending to diagnose.
records.content: Red-flag medical triage notebook is a practical offline routine for medical triage records. Create one page per person with name, age, known conditions, medicines, allergies, and emergency contact. Record time, main complaint, breathing, consciousness, bleeding, pain location, temperature if available, fluids taken, urine, and changes. Mark red flags: severe breathing trouble, chest pressure, stroke signs, uncontrolled bleeding, confusion, seizure, severe dehydration, severe allergic reaction, or worsening after injury. Put red-flag people at the top of the help list and keep someone watching them until professional help is reached. Update the page every 30 to 60 minutes during active illness or injury, and every shift during stable waiting. Write only facts observed, not guesses or blame. The goal is to make the action repeatable by a tired person, visible to helpers, and safe enough to stop when official help or a safer option appears.

records.long_term: Turn the notebook into a shift handover system so each helper can continue care without losing important details.

records.title: Medication shortage substitution decision log
records.summary: Documents medicine shortages safely without guessing substitutions or sharing medicines.
records.content: Medication shortage substitution decision log is a practical offline routine for medication continuity. List each medicine from its original label with person, remaining quantity, and prescriber if known. Mark medicines that the person was warned not to stop suddenly. Contact a pharmacist, doctor, clinic, or emergency line before changing dose or substitution. Count remaining days and warn before the last doses instead of waiting until empty. Store medicines by person and label, away from heat, moisture, children, and mixed containers.

records.summary: Creates a low-stimulation safety routine for panic, shock, grief, or agitation.
records.content: Mental crisis calm room watch is a practical offline routine for mental health support. Move the person away from crowds, arguments, bright lights, rumors, and repeated questions. Use a calm voice, short choices, and grounding facts: name, place, date, and next safe step. Remove obvious hazards without making the person feel trapped. Keep one trusted person nearby instead of a crowd of helpers. Escalate urgently if the person may harm self or others, cannot be kept safe, or has medical symptoms.
steps: Remove obvious hazards without making the person feel trapped.

records.title: Wound cleaning and infection watch routine
records.summary: A conservative routine for keeping minor wounds clean and watching for danger signs while seeking help for serious wounds.
records.content: Wound cleaning and infection watch routine is a practical offline routine for wound care records. Wash hands or use the cleanest available method before touching the wound. Rinse visible dirt from a minor wound with clean running water; do not scrub deep tissue. Cover with the cleanest dressing available and change it when wet, dirty, or loose. Circle redness lightly on skin or draw its size in the notebook with date and time. Watch for spreading redness, swelling, heat, pus, fever, red streaks, numbness, increasing pain, or bad smell. Seek medical help urgently for deep wounds, bites, dirty punctures, face/eye/genital wounds, heavy bleeding, or any worsening.
materials: Clean cloth or sterile gauze if available
warnings: Do not pour harsh chemicals into wounds.
Do not close deep or dirty wounds with glue, tape, or improvised stitches.
common_mistakes: Reusing dirty dressings.
Ignoring a wound because bleeding stopped.
Covering the wound without checking circulation and sensation nearby.
alternatives: Use freshly boiled-and-cooled cloth only when sterile supplies are unavailable.
Use a clean food bag as an outer moisture barrier, not directly as a dirty inner dressing.
failure_signs: Redness grows past the marked border.
Pain increases instead of decreasing.
The person develops fever, confusion, weakness, or red streaks.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat at home when the wound is severe, contaminated, caused by an animal/human bite, or bleeding heavily.
records.short_term: Clean, cover, label the time, and watch for danger signs.
records.long_term: Keep a dressing-change log and plan professional review if healing stalls or infection signs appear.
records.if_method_fails: If clean materials run out, prioritize handwashing, clean water, and covering only wounds at highest contamination risk.
records.environment_notes: Dust, floodwater, sewage, animal areas, and crowded shelters raise infection risk.

records.title: Asthma smoke exposure boundary
records.summary: A boundary card for people with asthma or breathing sensitivity when wildfire smoke, building smoke, dust, ash, or cleaning fumes begin to affect indoor air.
records.content: Core sequence: 1) Follow the person’s written asthma plan and keep rescue medicine, spacer, and contact numbers together. 2) Move away from smoke or fumes early; do not wait until speech, walking, or sleep is affected. 3) Reduce indoor smoke entry by closing obvious gaps and stopping activities that add dust or chemical vapors. 4) Escalate immediately if breathing becomes hard, lips or face change color, medicine is unavailable, or symptoms do not improve as expected.

records.title: Refrigerated medicine outage decision record
records.summary: Preserve time and temperature information and obtain product-specific advice instead of guessing whether a refrigerated medicine remains usable.
records.content: Action sequence: Keep the refrigerator closed and record the outage start time. Copy the medicine name, strength, form, storage range, batch, expiry, and whether it froze or was exposed to heat. Contact the pharmacist, prescriber, manufacturer, or emergency service for product-specific instructions. Separate questionable stock, label its exposure history, and replace it as soon as advised. Safety boundary: Do not discard a life-sustaining medicine or change its use without product-specific professional advice when help is reachable. Do not place medicine directly on ice or freeze it unless its official instructions explicitly allow that.

warnings: Do not discard a life-sustaining medicine or change its use without product-specific professional advice when help is reachable.

records.title: Seven-day medicine continuity sheet
records.summary: Create a portable, private record that lets a pharmacy or clinician quickly understand regular medicines and critical supply gaps.
records.content: Action sequence: List generic and brand name, strength, form, usual schedule, reason, prescriber, pharmacy, allergies, and last dose. Mark medicines that must not be stopped suddenly and those requiring refrigeration, monitoring, or special devices. Count the usable supply and write the date each item will run out at the usual schedule. Keep one protected paper copy with the person and one copy with a trusted contact. Safety boundary: Do not share the full list publicly or with people who do not need it. Do not ration, split, substitute, or change doses without qualified advice.
steps: List generic and brand name, strength, form, usual schedule, reason, prescriber, pharmacy, allergies, and last dose.
warnings: Do not share the full list publicly or with people who do not need it.

records.title: Poisoning call preparation in Greece
records.summary: Collect the container, exposure details, symptoms, and person information while immediately contacting the Greek Poison Centre or 112 as appropriate.
records.content: Action sequence: For collapse, breathing trouble, seizure, severe burns, or immediate danger call 112. Otherwise call the Greek Poison Centre at 210 7793777 and follow its instructions. State age, approximate weight, substance, amount, route, time, symptoms, first actions already taken, and exact location. Keep the product and packaging available and note every instruction and time. Safety boundary: Do not induce vomiting or give food, drink, medicine, or a home remedy unless the Poison Centre or emergency professional instructs it. Do not enter a contaminated area or touch the substance without appropriate protection.

records.title: Emergency pharmacy handover note
records.summary: Give a pharmacist a concise verified record so urgent continuity questions can be solved without relying on memory.
records.content: Action sequence: Separate confirmed information from what the person only remembers approximately. Present current medicines, allergies, last doses, remaining supply, storage exposure, and the exact reason continuity is at risk. Ask the pharmacist to write product-specific instructions, substitutions authorized by the prescriber, and the next review point. Update the household medicine sheet immediately after the handover. Safety boundary: Do not ask an unqualified person to identify loose tablets by appearance. Do not combine old and replacement instructions without confirming which plan is current.

records.title: Medicine go-bag rotation without missed doses
records.summary: Rotate emergency medicine stock through normal use with a written handover so the bag stays current without creating double dosing or shortages.

Move the oldest suitable stock into normal use only after the active supply and dosing schedule are confirmed. Replace the emergency quantity before removing the old stock and record package identifiers and new expiry dates. Have a second person compare the final bag with the current medicine list. Safety boundary: Do not store medicines in a hot vehicle, direct sun, damp bathroom, or unlabelled container. Do not create an emergency supply by skipping prescribed doses.

records.title: Child routine during disruption
records.summary: A structure for children that reduces fear, wandering, dehydration, and unsafe curiosity.
records.content: Children need truthful simple explanations, visible adults, small jobs, water reminders, and boundaries. A child routine can include wake time, wash time, safe play zone, quiet time, meal help, story time, and check-in words for fear. Give children jobs that help without exposing them to hazards. Do not use terrifying details as discipline.

Schedule water, toilet, rest, and reassurance.

records.title: Elder check-in card
records.summary: A simple card for checking hydration, heat/cold comfort, medicine timing, mobility, and mood.
records.content: Older adults may not complain loudly even when risk is rising. A check-in card makes quiet needs visible: water, food, medicine, toilet, walking safety, temperature comfort, pain, confusion, loneliness, and battery/contact needs. Keep the card respectful and private. Add a clear escalation rule: if the person misses two check-ins, sounds confused, lacks water, reports a fall, or cannot describe their location, the helper should involve a trusted neighbor, family contact, local service, or emergency support as appropriate. The card should also note pets, mobility aids, spare keys, and preferred language so help arrives faster and with less confusion.

Keep medicine in original packaging when possible, avoid freezing unless the label says so, protect from direct heat and sun, and ask a pharmacist or clinician for medicine-specific advice as soon as possible.

records.title: Foot care and blister prevention
records.summary: Protect feet during long walking, cleanup, shelter work, and wet conditions.
records.content: Foot problems can stop movement, cleanup, and caregiving. Keep feet dry, rotate socks, inspect pressure points, and deal with rubbing early. Do not cut blisters casually or walk on infected-looking wounds. People with diabetes, poor circulation, numbness, or immune problems need extra caution and qualified care when possible. For Foot care and blister prevention, the useful record should include the date, the person responsible, what was checked, what stayed uncertain, and the next safe action. Review foot care and blister prevention after weather changes, illness changes, new damage, new supplies, or movement to another place, because small changes can make an old decision unsafe.

records.title: Medicine continuity sheet
records.summary: A non-diagnostic record for medication names, timing, allergies, storage needs, supply, and refill routes during disruption.
records.content: Disasters hurt people with chronic conditions early. A medicine continuity sheet is not a prescription and must not replace medical advice. It is a memory and communication tool for doctors, pharmacists, responders, and caregivers. Copy medication names exactly from boxes, record dose and timing as prescribed, mark allergies clearly, note storage needs such as cooling, count remaining supply, and write the normal refill route. Keep one copy with the medicines and one smaller copy in a bag. Never change doses, stop essential medicine, or substitute unknown pills from rumor.

records.title: Community sanitation corner
records.summary: A low-tech place for handwashing, waste separation, cleaning tools, and illness prevention when normal services fail.
records.content: Sanitation collapses quietly: dirty hands near food, mixed waste, flies, bad smells, blocked drains, and children playing near contaminated water. A sanitation corner is a marked place that holds washing water, soap or clean ash when soap is absent, trash bags, cleaning tools, sharp-waste separation, and simple written rules. It must be far from drinking water and food preparation but close enough that people actually use it. The aim is routine, not perfection. Daily small cleaning prevents disease better than rare deep cleaning after the place is already disgusting.

records.content: Rumors fill silence. A rumor control board gives fear a place to be checked without shaming people. Use four columns: confirmed, unverified, questions, actions. Every item needs time and source, and old disproved items should be archived.

It prevents repeated fridge opening, rumor panic, battery waste, forgotten trash, and missed medication. It also gives children and stressed adults a predictable rhythm. The point is not military control; the point is to turn fear into small safe tasks that can be repeated.

records.title: Hand tool edge care
records.summary: A maintained cutting edge requires less force and is easier to control, but sharpening itself creates cut, flying-particle, and tool-failure hazards. This card covers inspection, restrained maintenance, verification, and safe storage for non-powered hand tools.
records.content:
Core procedure:
1. Identify the tool and its intended edge geometry; use the manufacturer’s maintenance instructions rather than guessing an angle or method. 2. Remove the tool from service and inspect the head, handle, fasteners, edge, and surrounding metal for cracks, looseness, mushrooming, deep chips, or corrosion. 3. Secure the tool so the edge faces away from the body and the work cannot slip; clear bystanders from the line of movement. 4. Use controlled strokes with the correct file or stone, preserving the original profile and removing only enough material to restore a continuous edge. 5. Remove loose filings, wipe and protect the surface as appropriate, then inspect for burrs, overheating marks, new cracks, or an uneven bevel. 6. Test control on suitable scrap material—not with a finger—then fit the guard, label any limitation, and record the date and work completed. Primary safety boundary: Do not sharpen or use a tool with a cracked head, loose or split handle, badly chipped edge, missing guard, or unknown heat damage. Fallback: If the correct sharpening tool or angle is unknown, clean and protect the item, mark it out of service, and refer it to a competent person.
materials: clean cloth and light protective oil where suitable
edge guard, sheath, or labelled storage rack
warnings: Do not sharpen or use a tool with a cracked head, loose or split handle, badly chipped edge, missing guard, or unknown heat damage.
Do not improvise high-speed grinding, change the original edge geometry, or work while the tool is unsupported or aimed toward another person.
common_mistakes: Testing sharpness by running a finger along the edge
Sharpening without first repairing a loose handle or damaged head
Removing too much metal or creating a thin overheated edge
Returning the tool to shared storage without a guard or status label
alternatives: If the correct sharpening tool or angle is unknown, clean and protect the item, mark it out of service, and refer it to a competent person.
Use a sound, correctly maintained replacement rather than forcing a damaged or blunt tool through the task.
failure_signs: The edge chips, rolls, cracks, or cannot hold its profile during a light scrap test
The handle, head, or fastener moves under hand pressure
Sharpening produces blue discoloration, uncontrolled heat, severe vibration, or flying fragments
when_not_to_use: Do not perform edge maintenance without the correct restraint, eye protection, lighting, and enough skill to follow the tool’s intended geometry.
Do not use this card for powered saws, grinding wheels, chainsaws, or specialised blades that require manufacturer servicing.
records.short_term: Inspect, restore, test, guard, and log one tool before returning it to service.
records.long_term: Maintain a tool register with inspection intervals, approved edge profiles, spare handles and guards, and named competent maintainers.
records.if_method_fails: Quarantine the tool, attach a clear defect note, and replace or professionally repair it; do not keep reshaping a failing edge.
records.environment_notes: Keep the bench dry and well lit, capture filings, protect others from the work zone, and prevent children from accessing tools or removed guards.

records.title: Manual pump care log
records.summary: A manual water pump should be checked by observation and recorded trends, not dismantled whenever output changes. This card creates a daily operating log, protects the water point from contamination, and defines when trained repair or water-quality action is required.
records.content:
Core procedure:
1. Identify the pump, water source, responsible operator, manufacturer guidance, and the normal number of strokes or time needed for a measured container. 2. Before operation, inspect the platform, drain, cover, handle, fasteners, spout, surrounding ground, and nearby contamination risks without opening sealed parts. 3. Pump normally and record date, operator, weather, approximate output, unusual resistance, noise, leakage, colour, odour, or visible sediment. 4. Keep the platform and drain clear, prevent containers from touching the spout, and stop animals, waste water, fuel, chemicals, or latrine runoff from reaching the source area. 5. Compare the reading with earlier entries; mark small changes for review and immediately isolate sudden output loss, structural damage, or suspected contamination. 6. At handover, list open faults, spare parts requested, water-use restrictions, samples or authority contacts, and the next scheduled inspection. Primary safety boundary: Do not assume clear-looking water is safe, and do not return a flooded, damaged, or contamination-suspected source to drinking use without competent assessment and required testing. Fallback: If output is unreliable, close the point, post the reason, and distribute water from a separately verified safe source.
materials: inspection checklist for the exact pump model
cleaning brush and approved surface-cleaning supplies
warnings: Do not assume clear-looking water is safe, and do not return a flooded, damaged, or contamination-suspected source to drinking use without competent assessment and required testing.
Do not open the wellhead, remove pump internals, add unapproved lubricant, or improvise parts unless trained for that exact pump and authorised to do so.
common_mistakes: Recording “working” without a measured output or observable condition
Cleaning the platform while allowing dirty water to drain back toward the source
Ignoring a gradual increase in strokes, leakage, or handle play
Mixing maintenance tools or lubricants with clean water containers
alternatives: If output is unreliable, close the point, post the reason, and distribute water from a separately verified safe source.
If no measuring vessel exists, use one dedicated clean container and record fill time consistently rather than estimating by eye.
failure_signs: Sudden loss of prime or output, severe handle looseness, cracked platform, open wellhead, or persistent abnormal noise
Floodwater, sewage, fuel, chemicals, dead animals, or heavy runoff near the source
New colour, odour, turbidity, sediment, illness cluster, or official notice questioning water safety
when_not_to_use: Do not use the pump for drinking water while contamination, structural damage, unsafe electrical equipment nearby, or an official restriction remains unresolved.
This log is not a repair manual and does not replace pump-specific maintenance instructions, trained technicians, water testing, or public-health direction.
records.short_term: Record one complete baseline check and clearly mark whether the source is open, restricted, or out of service.
records.long_term: Use dated trend records to schedule preventive maintenance, stock model-specific seals and fasteners, train at least two operators, and maintain a water-safety plan.
records.if_method_fails: Close and label the pump, protect the source from further contamination, notify the responsible water authority or trained repairer, and activate the verified alternate-water plan.
records.environment_notes: After flooding, earthquake damage, wildfire runoff, or chemical release, treat mechanical function and water safety as separate questions; a working pump can still deliver unsafe water.

records.title: Power bank cold-weather care
records.summary: Cold conditions can reduce the available output of a power bank, while charging a very cold, wet, damaged, or swollen lithium battery can create a serious failure risk. This card focuses on dry storage, gradual temperature recovery, inspection, conservative charging, and early isolation of warning signs.
records.content:
Core procedure:
1. Read the model’s permitted charging and storage temperatures; when those limits are unavailable, avoid charging while the unit is very cold or shows condensation. 2. Transport the power bank dry, protected from crushing and loose metal objects, and keep it close to the body or in an insulated bag without applying direct heat. 3. After entering a warmer area, leave the disconnected unit on a dry nonflammable surface until it has gradually warmed and all condensation has disappeared. 4. Inspect the case, ports, cable, and connectors for swelling, cracks, corrosion, liquid, unusual smell, looseness, or recalled-model information before use. 5. Charge only with compatible equipment in a visible, ventilated location away from bedding, paper, direct sun, heaters, and escape routes; check it periodically. 6. Record abnormal capacity loss or temperature, rotate healthy units rather than fully exhausting one, and store them according to the manufacturer’s state-of-charge guidance. Primary safety boundary: Stop using or charging a power bank that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, hissing, smoking, emitting vapour, or giving a strong unusual odour; move people away and call emergency services for fire or immediate danger. Fallback: If the unit cannot be safely warmed and inspected, keep it disconnected and use a verified spare battery or reduce phone power use.
materials: dry insulated pouch that does not trap a charging device
approved undamaged charging cable and adapter
separate fire-safe isolation area away from exits
warnings: Stop using or charging a power bank that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, hissing, smoking, emitting vapour, or giving a strong unusual odour; move people away and call emergency services for fire or immediate danger.
Do not heat a cold battery with flame, stove, radiator, hot water, hair dryer, or improvised heater, and do not charge it inside a sealed pouch or sleeping area.
common_mistakes: Charging immediately after bringing a frozen or condensation-covered unit indoors
Keeping keys, coins, or damaged cables against exposed connectors
Assuming rapid capacity loss is always harmless cold-weather behaviour
Charging unattended, under bedding, or in an evacuation route
alternatives: If the unit cannot be safely warmed and inspected, keep it disconnected and use a verified spare battery or reduce phone power use.
If no safe charging area exists, prioritise emergency communications and delay charging until a visible nonflammable location is available.
failure_signs: Swelling, case separation, leakage, corrosion, smoke, vapour, hissing, or a sharp chemical smell
Unexpected heating while idle or during a low-power charge
Repeated shutdowns, damaged ports, sparking, or capacity collapse after gradual warming
when_not_to_use: Do not reconnect a wet, physically damaged, recalled, or previously overheated power bank.
Do not attempt to open, puncture, flatten, freeze, repair, or dispose of a lithium battery in household fire or ordinary rubbish; follow local hazardous-battery instructions.

records.environment_notes: Wind chill does not cool an enclosed battery like exposed skin, but prolonged low temperature and condensation still matter; keep the unit dry and follow its documented limits.
